warmup.q: The ledger pool has 8 threads (core and max), a queue with room for 80 transfers, and a rule that turns the rest away. Each transfer takes 5 ms. 300 transfers arrive within a few milliseconds. About how many are accepted?
options: About 80: the size of the queue
warmup.why: From Inside ThreadPoolExecutor: core, max, queue, rejection: the 8 threads take the first 8 tasks, the next 80 fill the queue, and with core equal to max the pool can't add threads, so the other 212 are turned away. The demo in this lesson accepts 88 in most runs, because submitting 300 tasks takes less time than the first 5 ms transfer. On a very busy machine it can accept only 80, when the threads haven't picked up their first tasks before the queue fills.

opening:
Picture the bank at lunchtime on payday. Transfers arrive at 1,600 a second. Before the ledger changes any balance, it writes each transfer into a journal, a record on disk that survives a crash, and each write takes about 5 ms. The writing needs threads, paths of work that run side by side, so the ledger gets a thread pool: a fixed team of threads that take tasks from a queue, like the cooks and the order rail in Thread pools and executors.

How big should the team be, and how long the rail? One line, Executors.newFixedThreadPool(8), answers "eight cooks and a rail with no end". It passes every test. On the day the disk slows down, the rail grows by thousands of transfers a second, and each of them was told "accepted". At closing time, a plain shutdownNow() drops nearly all of them without a word.

Design the ledger and make it correct made the ledger right on any threads. This lesson chooses the threads. We'll size the pool from the bank's own numbers, close it without losing a transfer, publish balances that always add up, and find a stuck pool in a thread dump. Before we start, make a guess, and keep it in mind.
closing:
We started at the bank's busy hour with a pool nobody could explain. Now every number has a reason: 8 threads for 1,600 transfers a second at 5 ms, 80 slots for 50 ms of waiting, and a doorman who counts. A closing routine loses nothing, and snapshots always add up.

Now search your own code for Executors.newFixedThreadPool(, and for new LinkedBlockingQueue<>() with no size. Each one is a rail with no end. Write down how long it may grow, and what happens when it does.

Next, we'll serve thousands of customers at once. When every request mostly waits on a slow outside check, how do we give each one its own thread and still keep every limit?

sections.h: Every setting is a decision: sizing the pool from the bank's own numbers
sections.html:
Lesson 1's ledger is correct on any number of threads. Now it needs threads to run on. A real transfer does more than change two numbers. It first goes into the journal, a log on disk that the ledger writes before it changes anything in memory. If the program crashes, the journal still says which transfers were accepted, so none of them is lost. Say a journal write takes 5 ms.

Thread pools and executors pictured a pool as a kitchen: a team of cooks (the threads) taking tickets off a rail (the queue). The one-line pools each get one part of that kitchen wrong. Executors.newFixedThreadPool(8) has a rail with no end, so a slow disk turns into millions of waiting transfers and, finally, a program that runs out of memory. Executors.newCachedThreadPool() hires a new cook for every ticket, so the same slow disk turns into thousands of threads.

So we build the pool ourselves, and write down a reason for every setting:

Java
PoolPlan plan = PoolPlan.fromLittlesLaw(1_600, Duration.ofMillis(5), Duration.ofMillis(50));   // 8 and 80
ThreadPoolExecutor pool = new ThreadPoolExecutor(
        plan.threads(), plan.threads(),                    // core == max: no extra threads in a rush
        0, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS,
        new ArrayBlockingQueue<>(plan.queueCapacity()),    // bounded: a full queue says no
        Thread.ofPlatform().name("ledger-", 0).factory(),  // ledger-0, ledger-1, ... in every dump
        new CountingAbortPolicy());                        // counted, then thrown at the caller
pool.prestartAllCoreThreads();
Kotlin
val plan = PoolPlan.fromLittlesLaw(1_600, Duration.ofMillis(5), Duration.ofMillis(50))      // 8 and 80
val pool = ThreadPoolExecutor(
    plan.threads(), plan.threads(),                        // core == max: no extra threads in a rush
    0, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS,
    ArrayBlockingQueue(plan.queueCapacity()),              // bounded: a full queue says no
    Thread.ofPlatform().name("ledger-", 0).factory(),      // ledger-0, ledger-1, ... in every dump
    CountingAbortPolicy())                                 // counted, then thrown at the caller
pool.prestartAllCoreThreads()

The sizes come from Little's law, from Sizing a pool: CPU-bound, IO-bound and Little's law. It says the number of things inside a system equals the rate at which they arrive times how long each one stays. At the payday peak of 1,600 transfers a second, each holding a thread for 5 ms, that's 1,600 x 0.005 = 8 transfers in flight, that is, in progress at once. So we need 8 threads. With fewer, the queue grows at every peak. With many more, we only add threads that wait on the same disk.

The queue gets the same law. A busy pool finishes 1,600 transfers a second, so 80 queued transfers drain in 80 / 1,600 = 50 ms. If 50 ms is the longest a transfer should wait for a thread, 80 slots is the most the queue should hold. A queue of 10,000 would hide six seconds of waiting, long after the customer's app has given up.

A pool has a core size, the threads it keeps, and a maximum size, the most it may ever have. Core equals max here because, as Inside ThreadPoolExecutor showed, a pool adds threads past its core only when the queue is full. Extra threads would only add waiters on the same journal, so the right answer to a full queue is no.

That leaves the last decision: what happens to a transfer when the queue is full. That's the rejection policy. DiscardPolicy and DiscardOldestPolicy drop a transfer without telling anyone, so they are never right for money. CallerRunsPolicy makes the thread that submitted the transfer write the journal itself. That suits a nightly import, and it's wrong for a thread serving a customer who is waiting.

So the lab counts and throws. The counting policy is the bank's doorman. When the waiting area is full, he turns the next customer away politely and makes a mark on his clipboard. The customer gets a fast "busy, try again in a moment" (web servers send it as status 503) and tries again with the same transfer id. The marks show up on the bank's dashboard, the screen where its staff watch the program's numbers.

The thread factory gives each thread a name tag, ledger-0 to ledger-7, as Pools in production did for the kitchen's cooks. Those name tags will matter at the end of this lesson.

A pool you can't explain is a pool you can't trust. Write down a reason for every number.

The pool can take transfers now. The harder moment comes when it has to stop.

try.title: Send a burst at the pool
steps: Run BurstDemo: 300 transfers of 5 ms each arrive at once at the pool above. Predict how many are accepted, and how long submitting takes.
Run it with -Pargs=callerRuns. Predict how many transfers the submitting thread runs itself, and how long submitting takes now.

code.title: BurstDemo.java
code.html: package workbench.ledger.l02.demo; import java.util.concurrent.ArrayBlockingQueue; import java.util.concurrent.RejectedExecutionException; import java.util.concurrent.RejectedExecutionHandler; import java.util.concurrent.ThreadPoolExecutor; import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit; import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger; /** * A burst of 300 transfers hits a pool sized with Little's law: 8 threads, 80 queue slots, 5 ms * per transfer. Pass "callerRuns" to swap the counting abort policy for CallerRunsPolicy. */ public class BurstDemo { public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException { boolean callerRuns = args.length > 0 && args[0].equals("callerRuns"); AtomicInteger rejected = new AtomicInteger(); RejectedExecutionHandler policy = callerRuns ? new ThreadPoolExecutor.CallerRunsPolicy() // the submitting thread runs it itself : (task, pool) -> { // count it, then throw at the caller rejected.incrementAndGet(); throw new RejectedExecutionException("ledger pool full"); }; ThreadPoolExecutor pool = new ThreadPoolExecutor(8, 8, 0, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS, new ArrayBlockingQueue<>(80), Thread.ofPlatform().name("ledger-", 0).factory(), policy); pool.prestartAllCoreThreads(); AtomicInteger ranOnCaller = new AtomicInteger(); String caller = Thread.currentThread().getName(); long t0 = System.nanoTime(); int accepted = 0; for (int i = 0; i < 300; i++) { try { pool.execute(() -> { if (Thread.currentThread().getName().equals(caller)) ranOnCaller.incrementAndGet(); sleep(5); // the journal write }); accepted++; } catch (RejectedExecutionException e) { // a web server would answer "busy, try again soon" (status 503) here } } long submitMs = (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000; pool.shutdown(); pool.awaitTermination(10, TimeUnit.SECONDS); long doneMs = (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000; System.out.printf("%s: accepted %d, rejected %d, run by the submitting thread %d%n", callerRuns ? "CallerRunsPolicy" : "counting abort", accepted, rejected.get(), ranOnCaller.get()); System.out.printf("submitting took %d ms, all done after %d ms%n", submitMs, doneMs); } static void sleep(long ms) { try { Thread.sleep(ms); } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); } } }

Pass "callerRuns" to swap the counting abort policy for CallerRunsPolicy. */ fun main(args: Array<String>) { val callerRuns = args.firstOrNull() == "callerRuns" val rejected = AtomicInteger() val policy: RejectedExecutionHandler = if (callerRuns) ThreadPoolExecutor.CallerRunsPolicy() // the submitting thread runs it itself else RejectedExecutionHandler { _, _ -> // count it, then throw at the caller rejected.incrementAndGet() throw RejectedExecutionException("ledger pool full") } val pool = ThreadPoolExecutor(8, 8, 0, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS, ArrayBlockingQueue(80), Thread.ofPlatform().name("ledger-", 0).factory(), policy) pool.prestartAllCoreThreads() val ranOnCaller = AtomicInteger() val caller = Thread.currentThread().name val t0 = System.nanoTime() var accepted = 0 repeat(300) { try { pool.execute { if (Thread.currentThread().name == caller) ranOnCaller.incrementAndGet() Thread.sleep(5) // the journal write } accepted++ } catch (e: RejectedExecutionException) { // a web server would answer "busy, try again soon" (status 503) here } } val submitMs = (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000 pool.shutdown() pool.awaitTermination(10, TimeUnit.SECONDS) val doneMs = (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000 println("%s: accepted %d, rejected %d, run by the submitting thread %d" .format(if (callerRuns) "CallerRunsPolicy" else "counting abort", accepted, rejected.get(), ranOnCaller.get())) println("submitting took $submitMs ms, all done after $doneMs ms") }

try.expect: With the counting policy, 88 are accepted (8 running, 80 waiting) and 212 are turned away within a few milliseconds. On a very busy machine you may see 80, if the threads hadn't taken their first tasks before the queue filled. The accepted ones are done after roughly 60 to 70 ms (88 x 5 ms / 8 threads, plus start-up). With CallerRunsPolicy, nothing is turned away, but the submitting thread ran 24 or 25 transfers itself, and submitting took 131 to 141 ms instead of 5 to 8. While that thread writes a journal entry, it can't submit anything, which slows the stream down. If it were serving a customer, that customer would have waited the whole time for other people's transfers.

sections.h: Closing time: shutting down without losing a transfer
sections.html:
A new version of the bank's program goes live, and the old one has to stop while transfers are still queued. Each of them belongs to a customer who was told "accepted". So the rule for shutdown is simple to say. When it ends, every accepted transfer has been applied, has failed with an error its caller saw, or has been handed back to us by id. None may vanish.

pool.shutdownNow() on its own breaks that rule. It interrupts the running tasks, that is, asks them to stop, and returns the queued ones as a List<Runnable>. Ignore the list, and those transfers are gone. Worse, their futures never complete. A future is the takeaway ticket from Callable, Future, cancellation and interruption: the caller holds it, and waits on it with get() until the result is ready. Here is what this section's demo printed with a bare shutdownNow():

naive, grace 100 ms: accepted 1,000 | applied 0 | interrupted 8 | handed back 0 | lost 992
futures that will never complete: 992

Out of 1,000 accepted transfers, 992 simply vanished, and each one left a ticket that will never be called. A customer waiting on one of them would wait, very patiently, forever.

Pools in production closed the kitchen at night in order: stop taking orders, let the cooks finish within a deadline, then stop what's left and write it down. Here is that order for the ledger:

Java
public ShutdownReport shutdown(Duration grace) throws InterruptedException {
    pool.shutdown();                                              // 1. no new transfers; the queue drains
    if (pool.awaitTermination(grace.toNanos(), TimeUnit.NANOSECONDS))
        return new ShutdownReport(true, List.of());               // 2. everything accepted was applied
    List<Transfer> neverStarted = new ArrayList<>();
    for (Runnable r : pool.shutdownNow()) {                       // 3. interrupt, take back the queue
        TransferTask task = (TransferTask) r;
        task.cancel(false);                                       //    wakes a caller blocked in get()
        neverStarted.add(task.transfer());
    }
    pool.awaitTermination(grace.toNanos(), TimeUnit.NANOSECONDS);
    return new ShutdownReport(false, List.copyOf(neverStarted));  // 4. log them, or replay them
}
Kotlin
fun shutdown(grace: Duration): ShutdownReport {
    pool.shutdown()                                               // 1. no new transfers; the queue drains
    if (pool.awaitTermination(grace.toNanos(), TimeUnit.NANOSECONDS))
        return ShutdownReport(true, emptyList())                  // 2. everything accepted was applied
    val neverStarted = pool.shutdownNow().map { r ->              // 3. interrupt, take back the queue
        val task = r as TransferTask
        task.cancel(false)                                        //    wakes a caller blocked in get()
        task.transfer
    }
    pool.awaitTermination(grace.toNanos(), TimeUnit.NANOSECONDS)
    return ShutdownReport(false, neverStarted)                    // 4. log them, or replay them
}

First, shutdown() closes the door to new transfers, while the queue keeps draining (1). Then we wait up to the grace period, the time we allow for draining. If the pool finished, everything accepted was applied (2). If not, shutdownNow() interrupts the running transfers and hands back the queue (3). We cancel each queued task, which completes its future, so a caller blocked in get() wakes up with a CancellationException instead of waiting forever. Finally, we wait once more and report the transfers that never started, so someone can log them or run them again later (4).

Two details make this work. First, the queue must hold objects that know their transfer. pool.submit(callable) wraps your work in an anonymous FutureTask, so the lab's submit builds a TransferTask, a FutureTask that remembers its transfer, and hands it to execute. Then shutdownNow() gives back transfers, not mystery Runnables.

Second, an interrupted task must leave nothing half done. Each task writes the journal first and changes memory second. An interrupt during the journal write means the transfer was never applied: its future fails, and no balance changed. And apply itself never waits for anything, so once it starts, it finishes.

The grace period comes from the same numbers as the pool. A full queue of 80 drains in 50 ms, so a few seconds of grace is plenty. The system that stops a program for a new version usually waits about 30 seconds before it stops it by force, and the drain fits easily inside that. With the drain in place, the same demo printed:

drain, grace 100 ms: accepted 1,000 | applied 157 | interrupted 8 | handed back 835 | lost 0
futures that will never complete: 0

The arithmetic holds: 100 ms is 20 rounds of 5 ms on 8 threads, about 160 transfers. Eight were stopped in the middle of their journal write, and the other 835 came back by id.

Shutdown is part of the program. Drain first, then hand back what never ran.

No transfer goes missing at closing time now. But a customer who asks for every balance at once can still see a number that never existed.

try.title: Lose transfers, then stop losing them
steps: Run ShutdownDemo -Pargs=naive: 1,000 accepted transfers, then a bare shutdownNow(). Read the lost column and the last line.
Run it with no arguments (drain, 100 ms of grace), then with -Pargs='drain 5000'. Before each run, predict how many transfers are applied.

code.title: ShutdownDemo.java
code.html: package workbench.ledger.l02.demo; import java.util.ArrayList; import java.util.List; import java.util.concurrent.ArrayBlockingQueue; import java.util.concurrent.Callable; import java.util.concurrent.FutureTask; import java.util.concurrent.ThreadPoolExecutor; import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit; import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger; /** * 1,000 transfers wait on 8 threads at 5 ms each, then the service stops. Where does each one end up? * Args: "naive" or "drain" (the default), then the grace period in ms (default 100). */ public class ShutdownDemo { record Transfer(int id) {} // a FutureTask that remembers its transfer, so the queue hands back transfers, not anonymous Runnables static final class TransferTask extends FutureTask<Boolean> { final Transfer transfer; TransferTask(Transfer transfer, Callable<Boolean> work) { super(work); this.transfer = transfer; } } public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException { String mode = args.length > 0 ? args[0] : "drain"; long graceMs = args.length > 1 ? Long.parseLong(args[1]) : 100; ThreadPoolExecutor pool = new ThreadPoolExecutor(8, 8, 0, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS, new ArrayBlockingQueue<>(1_000), Thread.ofPlatform().name("ledger-", 0).factory()); AtomicInteger applied = new AtomicInteger(), interrupted = new AtomicInteger(); List<TransferTask> accepted = new ArrayList<>(); for (int i = 0; i < 1_000; i++) { TransferTask task = new TransferTask(new Transfer(i), () -> { try { Thread.sleep(5); // the journal write } catch (InterruptedException e) { interrupted.incrementAndGet(); // not journaled, so not applied throw e; } applied.incrementAndGet(); return true; }); pool.execute(task); accepted.add(task); } int handedBack = 0; if (mode.equals("naive")) { pool.shutdownNow(); // the list of queued tasks it returns is dropped } else { pool.shutdown(); // 1. no new work; the queue keeps draining if (!pool.awaitTermination(graceMs, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS)) { List<Runnable> neverStarted = pool.shutdownNow(); // 2. interrupt, take back the queue for (Runnable r : neverStarted) ((TransferTask) r).cancel(false); // 3. wake anyone waiting on them handedBack = neverStarted.size(); // 4. log these ids, or replay them on restart } } pool.awaitTermination(5, TimeUnit.SECONDS); long neverComplete = accepted.stream().filter(t -> !t.isDone()).count(); System.out.printf("%s, grace %d ms: accepted 1,000 | applied %,d | interrupted %d | handed back %,d | lost %,d%n", mode, graceMs, applied.get(), interrupted.get(), handedBack, 1_000 - applied.get() - interrupted.get() - handedBack); System.out.printf("futures that will never complete: %,d%n", neverComplete); } }

try.expect: Naive: about 990 lost (987 and 992 in runs here), and as many futures that will never complete, so their callers would wait forever. Drain with 100 ms: about 160 applied (8 threads x 20 rounds of 5 ms), 7 or 8 interrupted in the middle of their journal write, 835 handed back, and 0 lost. With 5 s of grace, all 1,000 are applied, because they need only about 625 ms on 8 threads.

sections.h: A snapshot of every balance, published so nobody sees it torn
sections.html:
The bank's app has a page that shows every balance at once, and rule 1 says they must add up to the opening total. Let's try the obvious way on a small ledger: 50 accounts with 1,000 cents each, so 50,000 in total. A reader walks the accounts in id order. It locks one account, reads it, adds it and moves on:

Java
long sum = 0;
for (Account a : accounts) {
    a.lock().lock();
    try { sum += a.balance(); } finally { a.lock().unlock(); }   // each read is safe...
}                                                                  // ...the sum is not
Kotlin
var sum = 0L
for (a in accounts) {
    sum += a.lock.withLock { a.balance }                         // each read is safe...
}                                                                  // ...the sum is not

Trace the smallest case. The reader has already passed account 3. Now a transfer moves 300 cents from account 40 to account 3. The reader goes on and reads the rest, account 40 included, and gets 49,700. It saw account 3 before the money arrived, and account 40 after it left. Every read held a lock, and no transfer broke a rule. The sum still mixes two moments. A sum like that is torn: it matches no state the ledger was ever in. A transfer in the other direction makes the reader count the same money twice.

In one Java run of this section's demo, 7,241 of 9,456 sums were torn, some by thousands of cents. Runs on a busier machine tore fewer, 368 to 506 sums out of thousands, but never none.

A whole snapshot needs one moment at which no transfer is half done. Don't share: immutability, confinement, ThreadLocal gave us the picture. The shop owner doesn't erase prices while people read the board; she prints a new board and hangs it up in one move. For the ledger, that means taking every account's lock, in the same id order that apply uses, so a snapshot can never deadlock with a transfer. Then we copy the balances into a new record that never changes, publish it, and let go:

Java
public BalanceSnapshot snapshot() {
    for (Account a : inLockOrder) a.lock().lock();                 // 1. every lock, in id order
    try {
        Map<String, Long> copy = new HashMap<>();
        long total = 0;
        for (Account a : inLockOrder) { copy.put(a.id(), a.balance()); total += a.balance(); }
        BalanceSnapshot s = new BalanceSnapshot(copy, total, ++version);   // 2. a record that never changes
        latest = s;                                                // 3. one volatile write publishes it
        return s;
    } finally {
        for (int i = inLockOrder.size() - 1; i >= 0; i--) inLockOrder.get(i).lock().unlock();
    }
}
Kotlin
fun snapshot(): BalanceSnapshot {
    inLockOrder.forEach { it.lock.lock() }                         // 1. every lock, in id order
    try {
        val copy = inLockOrder.associate { it.id to it.balance }
        val s = BalanceSnapshot(copy, copy.values.sum(), ++version) // 2. a record that never changes
        latest = s                                                 // 3. one @Volatile write publishes it
        return s
    } finally {
        inLockOrder.asReversed().forEach { it.lock.unlock() }
    }
}

First we take every lock, in id order (1). Now no transfer can move money. Then we copy all 50 balances into a new record, with the total and a version number (2). Then one write to latest publishes it (3). The keyword volatile marks a field whose every read sees the latest write, from any thread. Last, the finally releases the locks in reverse order, and any transfer that was waiting runs.

Readers stop adding things up. They read one field, latest, which points to the last finished snapshot, and they take no lock at all. A reader who looks just before a new snapshot is published sees all of the old one: old, but whole. A reader who looks just after sees all of the new one. Old or new, never a mix.

Happens-before, the rules that matter, asked us to name the rule that makes each shared field safe to read. Here is the list for the whole ledger:

Field Why every reader sees it correctly
Account.balance the account's lock: each release happens-before the next lock of the same account
accounts, inLockOrder final fields, set in the constructor, never changed
version written only while every account lock is held
latest volatile: its write happens-before every later read
a snapshot's balances and total final fields of a record, holding a map that Map.copyOf made unchangeable
a Transfer in the pool it never changes, and execute happens-before the task runs
a transfer's outcome the task's end happens-before Future.get() returns

Three pictures from the memory model track sit in that table. The account locks are the cashier's key: whoever takes the same key next sees everything written before it was handed on. latest is the museum's OPEN/CLOSED sign, a volatile field that every reader checks fresh. And a finished BalanceSnapshot is a letter in a sealed envelope, whole for anyone who receives it.

Writing latest before the locks are released keeps snapshots in version order. Two snapshots can't overlap, because each one needs every lock.

Build the whole snapshot while no transfer can run, then publish it with one volatile write.

Every field now has a named rule behind it. One last kind of failure has no field at all: a pool that waits for itself.

try.title: Tear a snapshot, then make it whole
steps: Run TornSnapshotDemo. Four threads move money while the main thread adds up all 50 balances, one locked account at a time. Predict how many sums come out wrong.
Run it with -Pargs=locked, where the reader holds every lock while it adds.

code.title: TornSnapshotDemo.java
code.html: package workbench.ledger.l02.demo; import java.util.ArrayList; import java.util.List; import java.util.concurrent.ThreadLocalRandom; import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicBoolean; import java.util.concurrent.locks.ReentrantLock; /** * Four threads move money between 50 accounts while a reader adds up all the balances. * Pass "locked" to make the reader hold every account lock while it adds. */ public class TornSnapshotDemo { static final class Account { final int id; final ReentrantLock lock = new ReentrantLock(); long balance = 1_000; // guarded by lock: 50,000 in total Account(int id) { this.id = id; } } public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException { boolean locked = args.length > 0 && args[0].equals("locked"); Account[] accounts = new Account[50]; for (int i = 0; i < accounts.length; i++) accounts[i] = new Account(i); AtomicBoolean writing = new AtomicBoolean(true); List<Thread> writers = new ArrayList<>(); for (int w = 0; w < 4; w++) { writers.add(Thread.ofPlatform().start(() -> { ThreadLocalRandom rnd = ThreadLocalRandom.current(); for (int n = 0; n < 200_000; n++) { int a = rnd.nextInt(50), b = rnd.nextInt(49); if (b >= a) b++; move(accounts[a], accounts[b], 1 + rnd.nextLong(500)); } })); } long taken = 0, torn = 0, worst = 0; while (writers.stream().anyMatch(Thread::isAlive)) { long sum = locked ? sumAllLocked(accounts) : sumOneByOne(accounts); taken++; if (sum != 50_000) { torn++; worst = Math.max(worst, Math.abs(sum - 50_000)); } } System.out.printf("%s: %,d snapshots, %,d torn (worst off by %,d cents)%n", locked ? "every lock held" : "one account at a time", taken, torn, worst); } // each read is safe on its own; the sum is not, because money moves between reads static long sumOneByOne(Account[] accounts) { long sum = 0; for (Account a : accounts) { a.lock.lock(); try { sum += a.balance; } finally { a.lock.unlock(); } } return sum; } // every lock, in id order: no transfer can run while we add, so the sum is one instant static long sumAllLocked(Account[] accounts) { for (Account a : accounts) a.lock.lock(); try { long sum = 0; for (Account a : accounts) sum += a.balance; return sum; } finally { for (int i = accounts.length - 1; i >= 0; i--) accounts[i].lock.unlock(); } } static void move(Account from, Account to, long cents) { Account first = from.id < to.id ? from : to, second = first == from ? to : from; first.lock.lock(); try { second.lock.lock(); try { if (from.balance >= cents) { from.balance -= cents; to.balance += cents; } } finally { second.lock.unlock(); } } finally { first.lock.unlock(); } } }

alt.title: TornSnapshotDemo.kt
alt.html: package workbench.ledger.l02.demo import java.util.concurrent.ThreadLocalRandom import java.util.concurrent.locks.ReentrantLock import kotlin.concurrent.withLock private class SnapshotAccount(val id: Int) { val lock = ReentrantLock() var balance = 1_000L // guarded by lock: 50,000 in total } /** * Four threads move money between 50 accounts while a reader adds up all the balances. * Pass "locked" to make the reader hold every account lock while it adds. */ fun main(args: Array<String>) { val locked = args.firstOrNull() == "locked" val accounts = Array(50) { SnapshotAccount(it) } val writers = List(4) { Thread.ofPlatform().start { val rnd = ThreadLocalRandom.current() repeat(200_000) { val a = rnd.nextInt(50) var b = rnd.nextInt(49) if (b >= a) b++ move(accounts[a], accounts[b], 1 + rnd.nextLong(500)) } } } var taken = 0L var torn = 0L var worst = 0L while (writers.any { it.isAlive }) { val sum = if (locked) sumAllLocked(accounts) else sumOneByOne(accounts) taken++ if (sum != 50_000L) { torn++ worst = maxOf(worst, Math.abs(sum - 50_000)) } } println("%s: %,d snapshots, %,d torn (worst off by %,d cents)" .format(if (locked) "every lock held" else "one account at a time", taken, torn, worst)) } // each read is safe on its own; the sum is not, because money moves between reads private fun sumOneByOne(accounts: Array<SnapshotAccount>): Long = accounts.sumOf { a -> a.lock.withLock { a.balance } } // every lock, in id order: no transfer can run while we add, so the sum is one instant private fun sumAllLocked(accounts: Array<SnapshotAccount>): Long { accounts.forEach { it.lock.lock() } try { return accounts.sumOf { it.balance } } finally { accounts.reversed().forEach { it.lock.unlock() } } } private fun move(from: SnapshotAccount, to: SnapshotAccount, cents: Long) { val first = if (from.id < to.id) from else to val second = if (first === from) to else from first.lock.withLock { second.lock.withLock { if (from.balance >= cents) { from.balance -= cents; to.balance += cents } } } }

try.expect: One account at a time, a good share of the sums are wrong: 7,241 of 9,456 in one Java run, and 506 of 4,607 and 368 of 9,422 in Java and Kotlin runs on a busier machine, some off by more than 7,000 cents, while every transfer kept the books balanced. With every lock held, no sum is torn. A real bank wouldn't let every request take all the locks. It takes one snapshot every few hundred milliseconds and lets readers share it through latestSnapshot().

aside.title: Doesn't locking all 50 accounts stop the bank?
aside.html: For a moment, yes, and the moment is short. Copying 50 balances takes microseconds, so a transfer that arrives meanwhile waits about as long as it would behind one busy account. The cost grows with the number of accounts, though, and at five million accounts holding every lock would be a pause customers feel. Real systems then take snapshots less often, or split the accounts into groups with a snapshot each, or build snapshots from the journal on another machine. Go deeper, at the end of this lesson, sketches all three.

video.title: Locked reads one account at a time are a panorama, and the sum tears; a snapshot takes every lock in id order, copies into a record that never changes, and publishes it with one volatile write, so readers see old or new, never a mix

sections.h: A stuck pool, found in a thread dump
sections.html:
Here is a bug that passes every test with a small batch. At the end of each month, the bank prints a statement for every account, a page that shows its balance. The statement job runs on the ledger pool, and each statement asks the same pool for the balance:

Java
pool.submit(() -> {
    Future<Long> balance = pool.submit(() -> balanceOf(account));    // a task inside a task
    return account + ": " + balance.get();                           // waits for it
});
Kotlin
pool.submit(Callable {
    val balance = pool.submit(Callable { balanceOf(account) })       // a task inside a task
    "$account: ${balance.get()}"                                     // waits for it
})

With 2 threads and 3 statements, the first two statements take both threads. Each one submits a balance lookup, which joins the queue behind the third statement. Now both threads wait for lookups that need a free thread, and no thread will ever be free. Pools in production called this pool-induced deadlock, and pictured it as cooks waiting for tickets that sit on the rail behind them. This section is about finding it in a running program.

The tool is jcmd, which comes with the JDK and sends commands to a running Java program. One of its commands prints a thread dump: every thread's name, state and stack (the chain of method calls it is in the middle of) at one moment. Start PoolHangDemo with a long hang, then run this from a second terminal:

jcmd                          # lists running Java programs and their process ids
jcmd <pid> Thread.print -l    # -l adds the java.util.concurrent locks each thread holds

Here's the part that matters, from a real run on JDK 21, trimmed:

"ledger-0" #19 [5741] prio=5 os_prio=0 cpu=1.33ms elapsed=1.74s ... waiting on condition
   java.lang.Thread.State: WAITING (parking)
	at jdk.internal.misc.Unsafe.park(java.base@21.0.12.1/Native Method)
	- parking to wait for  <0x00000006f79ef530> (a java.util.concurrent.FutureTask)
	at java.util.concurrent.locks.LockSupport.park(java.base@21.0.12.1/LockSupport.java:221)
	at java.util.concurrent.FutureTask.awaitDone(java.base@21.0.12.1/FutureTask.java:500)
	at java.util.concurrent.FutureTask.get(java.base@21.0.12.1/FutureTask.java:190)
	at workbench.ledger.l02.demo.PoolHangDemo.statement(PoolHangDemo.java:33)
	at workbench.ledger.l02.demo.PoolHangDemo.lambda$main$0(PoolHangDemo.java:21)
	...
	at java.util.concurrent.ThreadPoolExecutor.runWorker(java.base@21.0.12.1/ThreadPoolExecutor.java:1144)
	...
   Locked ownable synchronizers:
	- <0x00000006f79650b8> (a java.util.concurrent.ThreadPoolExecutor$Worker)

"ledger-1" #20 [5742] prio=5 os_prio=0 cpu=0.83ms elapsed=1.74s ... waiting on condition
   java.lang.Thread.State: WAITING (parking)
	at jdk.internal.misc.Unsafe.park(java.base@21.0.12.1/Native Method)
	- parking to wait for  <0x00000006f7602c18> (a java.util.concurrent.FutureTask)
	...
	at workbench.ledger.l02.demo.PoolHangDemo.statement(PoolHangDemo.java:33)
	...
   Locked ownable synchronizers:
	- <0x00000006f79bb838> (a java.util.concurrent.ThreadPoolExecutor$Worker)

Read each thread in the same order. The name says which pool: both ledger- threads are stuck, and their name tags tell us so at once. The state, WAITING (parking), means a java.util.concurrent tool put them to sleep; a thread stuck at a synchronized block would say BLOCKED. The parking to wait for line names the object they wait on, a FutureTask, so they are inside get(). The first line from our own code, statement at line 33, is that get() call. And under Locked ownable synchronizers, each thread holds its own ThreadPoolExecutor$Worker, a lock that a pool thread holds while it runs a task. Both threads are busy, and busy waiting.

Notice what's missing: the dump never says Found one Java-level deadlock. The JVM's detector looks for threads that hold locks other threads want, in a circle. Here nobody holds a lock that anybody else wants. So learn this signature instead: every thread of one pool parked on a FutureTask from that same pool, with tasks still queued. The fixes come from that lesson. Do the lookup inline, chain the next step with thenApply instead of waiting, or give lookups their own pool.

A pool whose tasks wait on the same pool can stop without any lock. Never wait on your own pool from inside it.

This pool is right for the journal writes, which are short and few at a time. It would be wrong for the customers' requests themselves. A request spends most of its time waiting on other services, and a pool of platform threads, the ordinary threads the operating system runs, can hold only a few hundred waiting requests. That's the next sitting's job.

try.title: Take the dump yourself
steps: Run PoolHangDemo with -Pargs=60 so it stays stuck for a minute. It prints its process id.

In a second terminal, run jcmd <pid> Thread.print -l. For both ledger- threads, find the state, the parking to wait for line, the first line from workbench.ledger, and the Locked ownable synchronizers. Then find main.
Scroll to the end of the dump. Is there a deadlock report? Explain why not.
Change statement to call balanceOf(account) directly instead of submitting it, and run the demo again.

code.title: PoolHangDemo.java
code.html: package workbench.ledger.l02.demo; import java.util.List; import java.util.concurrent.ArrayBlockingQueue; import java.util.concurrent.ExecutorService; import java.util.concurrent.Future; import java.util.concurrent.ThreadPoolExecutor; import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit; /** * Month-end statements on the ledger pool: each statement task asks the same 2-thread pool for a * balance and waits for the answer. Run it, then take a thread dump while it hangs. * Arg: how many seconds to stay hung (default 4). */ public class PoolHangDemo { public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException { int seconds = args.length > 0 ? Integer.parseInt(args[0]) : 4; ThreadPoolExecutor pool = new ThreadPoolExecutor(2, 2, 0, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS, new ArrayBlockingQueue<>(100), Thread.ofPlatform().name("ledger-", 0).factory()); for (String account : List.of("acc-01", "acc-02", "acc-03")) { pool.submit(() -> statement(pool, account)); } long pid = ProcessHandle.current().pid(); System.out.printf("pid %d, hanging for %d s. In another terminal: jcmd %d Thread.print -l%n", pid, seconds, pid); Thread.sleep(seconds * 1_000L); System.out.printf("after %d s: active=%d, queued=%d, completed=%d%n", seconds, pool.getActiveCount(), pool.getQueue().size(), pool.getCompletedTaskCount()); pool.shutdownNow(); // interrupts the two get() calls that will never return } static String statement(ExecutorService pool, String account) throws Exception { Future<Long> balance = pool.submit(() -> balanceOf(account)); // queued behind the other statements return account + ": " + balance.get(); // waits for a thread that is never free } static long balanceOf(String account) { return 4_200; // fast: the problem is not speed } }

alt.title: PoolHangDemo.kt
alt.html: package workbench.ledger.l02.demo import java.util.concurrent.ArrayBlockingQueue import java.util.concurrent.Callable import java.util.concurrent.ExecutorService import java.util.concurrent.ThreadPoolExecutor import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit /** * Month-end statements on the ledger pool: each statement task asks the same 2-thread pool for a * balance and waits for the answer. Run it, then take a thread dump while it hangs. * Arg: how many seconds to stay hung (default 4). */ fun main(args: Array<String>) { val seconds = args.firstOrNull()?.toInt() ?: 4 val pool = ThreadPoolExecutor(2, 2, 0, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS, ArrayBlockingQueue(100), Thread.ofPlatform().name("ledger-", 0).factory()) for (account in listOf("acc-01", "acc-02", "acc-03")) { pool.submit(Callable { statement(pool, account) }) } val pid = ProcessHandle.current().pid() println("pid $pid, hanging for $seconds s. In another terminal: jcmd $pid Thread.print -l") Thread.sleep(seconds * 1_000L) println("after $seconds s: active=${pool.activeCount}, queued=${pool.queue.size}, completed=${pool.completedTaskCount}") pool.shutdownNow() // interrupts the two get() calls that will never return } private fun statement(pool: ExecutorService, account: String): String { val balance = pool.submit(Callable { balanceOf(account) }) // queued behind the other statements return "$account: ${balance.get()}" // waits for a thread that is never free } private fun balanceOf(account: String): Long = 4_200 // fast: the problem is not speed

try.expect: Both ledger-0 and ledger-1 are WAITING (parking) on a FutureTask inside PoolHangDemo.statement, each holding its ThreadPoolExecutor$Worker, and main is TIMED_WAITING (sleeping) in Thread.sleep. There is no deadlock report, because no thread holds a lock another thread wants. When the sleep ends, the demo prints active=2, queued=3, completed=0: the third statement and both lookups never ran. With the lookup inline, it prints completed=3. The Kotlin twin shows the same dump, with PoolHangDemoKt.statement as your line.

compare.title: Starting the pool and submitting a transfer

java.title: LedgerService.java
java.html: public static LedgerService start(Ledger ledger, Journal journal, PoolPlan plan) { CountingAbortPolicy rejections = new CountingAbortPolicy(); ThreadPoolExecutor pool = new ThreadPoolExecutor( plan.threads(), plan.threads(), 0, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS, new ArrayBlockingQueue<>(plan.queueCapacity()), Thread.ofPlatform().name("ledger-", 0).factory(), rejections); pool.prestartAllCoreThreads(); return new LedgerService(ledger, journal, pool, rejections); } public Future<Outcome> submit(Transfer t) { TransferTask task = new TransferTask(t, () -> { journal.append(t); return ledger.apply(t); }); pool.execute(task); return task; } static final class TransferTask extends FutureTask<Outcome> { private final Transfer transfer; TransferTask(Transfer transfer, Callable<Outcome> work) { super(work); this.transfer = transfer; } Transfer transfer() { return transfer; } }

kotlin.title: LedgerService.kt
kotlin.html: fun start(ledger: Ledger, journal: Journal, plan: PoolPlan): LedgerService { val rejections = CountingAbortPolicy() val pool = ThreadPoolExecutor( plan.threads, plan.threads, 0, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS, ArrayBlockingQueue(plan.queueCapacity), Thread.ofPlatform().name("ledger-", 0).factory(), rejections) pool.prestartAllCoreThreads() return LedgerService(ledger, journal, pool, rejections) } fun submit(t: Transfer): Future<Outcome> { val task = TransferTask(t) { journal.append(t) ledger.apply(t) } pool.execute(task) return task } class TransferTask(val transfer: Transfer, work: Callable<Outcome>) : FutureTask<Outcome>(work)

compare.note: Nothing here is special to either language: ThreadPoolExecutor, ArrayBlockingQueue and Thread.ofPlatform() are the same JDK classes, with the same rules. Kotlin shortens the FutureTask subclass to one line, because the constructor parameter work goes straight to the parent class in the class header, and a trailing lambda becomes the Java Callable. One Kotlin detail matters. When you call pool.submit with a bare lambda, Kotlin has to choose between submit(Runnable) and submit(Callable). Writing Callable { ... } says which one you mean, so the future carries your result.

worked.title: Size the pool for a busier payday

steps.say: The bank expects a busier payday: 4,000 transfers a second at the peak. Under that load, a journal write takes 4 ms. We want no transfer to wait more than 100 ms for a thread. Start with Little's law, for both halves of the pool.
steps.code: // 1. peak rate, time each transfer holds a thread, longest acceptable wait in the queue PoolPlan plan = PoolPlan.fromLittlesLaw(4_000, Duration.ofMillis(4), Duration.ofMillis(100)); // 2. 4,000/s x 0.004 s = 16 in flight; 4,000/s x 0.1 s = 400 waiting System.out.println(plan); // PoolPlan[threads=16, queueCapacity=400]

alt.html: // 1. peak rate, time each transfer holds a thread, longest acceptable wait in the queue val plan = PoolPlan.fromLittlesLaw(4_000, Duration.ofMillis(4), Duration.ofMillis(100)) // 2. 4,000/s x 0.004 s = 16 in flight; 4,000/s x 0.1 s = 400 waiting println(plan) // PoolPlan[threads=16, queueCapacity=400]

steps.say: Now check what sits behind the pool, as Sizing a pool insisted. The disk that holds the journal handles 12 writes at once before each one slows down. With 16 threads, the extra 4 only queue inside the journal and make every write slower. The real ceiling is the journal's: 12 writes / 0.004 s = 3,000 transfers a second, whatever the forecast says.

Size from the scarce resource, and let the rejection policy handle the rest. At 3,000 a second, 100 ms of waiting is 300 slots. Above that rate, the doorman turns transfers away and counts them, and customers get a fast "busy, try again".
steps.code: // 3. the journal takes 12 writes at once: that sets the threads, and the throughput PoolPlan capped = new PoolPlan(12, 300); // 12 / 0.004 s = 3,000 a second; 3,000 x 0.1 s = 300 slots LedgerService service = LedgerService.start(ledger, journal, capped);

alt.html: // 3. the journal takes 12 writes at once: that sets the threads, and the throughput val capped = PoolPlan(12, 300) // 12 / 0.004 s = 3,000 a second; 3,000 x 0.1 s = 300 slots val service = LedgerService.start(ledger, journal, capped)

steps.say: If 3,000 isn't enough, more threads won't help, because the journal is the bottleneck, the narrowest point everything passes through. Make each write carry more instead. Writing a batch of transfers to disk in one go (often called group commit) raises what 12 writes at once can carry. Then check shutdown again: 300 queued transfers on 12 threads at 4 ms drain in 100 ms, so a 5 s grace period still fits well inside the usual 30 s.

lab.title: Put the ledger on a pool, drain it, and publish snapshots
steps: Run the tests once. All eight fail. Ledger.apply is already lesson 1's solution. Read the comments at the top of Ledger: they name the happens-before rule for every field, like the table in the snapshot section.
Write PoolPlan.fromLittlesLaw, Little's law in whole numbers: Math.ceilDiv(perSecond * d.toNanos(), 1_000_000_000L) for both numbers, and never less than 1.

Write LedgerService.start (the pool from the first section), submit (a TransferTask that writes the journal and then applies, passed to pool.execute) and CountingAbortPolicy.rejectedExecution (count, then throw).
Write LedgerService.shutdown in the closing-time order: shutdown, awaitTermination, then shutdownNow; cancel and collect each TransferTask, wait once more, and report.
Write Ledger.snapshot: lock every account in inLockOrder, copy the balances, build the snapshot with ++version, write latest, and release the locks in reverse order in a finally.
Run the tests until all eight pass, then twice more.
hints: Use pool.execute(task), not pool.submit(task). submit would wrap your TransferTask in another FutureTask, and shutdownNow() would hand back that wrapper.
The shutdown test's journal waits until it is interrupted. If your shutdown hangs, check that you call shutdownNow() when the first awaitTermination returns false.
If the torn-snapshot test fails, check that you take every lock before you read any balance, and release none until the snapshot is built and published.
perSecond * timePerTransfer.toNanos() multiplies an int by a long, so Java computes it as a long. It doesn't overflow at these sizes.
lab.done: All eight tests in LedgerServiceTest pass, three runs in a row.

drill.title: Write the drain-then-hand-back shutdown from memory
drill.prompt: Close the lab. Write List<Runnable> stop(ExecutorService pool, Duration grace): stop taking new work, let the queue drain for at most grace, then interrupt what is still running and return the tasks that never started, after cancelling any of them that are futures. If you are interrupted while waiting, keep the interrupt flag set.

answer.html: List<Runnable> stop(ExecutorService pool, Duration grace) { pool.shutdown(); // no new work; the queue keeps draining try { if (pool.awaitTermination(grace.toNanos(), TimeUnit.NANOSECONDS)) return List.of(); } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); // keep the flag, then stop hard } List<Runnable> neverStarted = pool.shutdownNow(); // interrupts the running tasks for (Runnable r : neverStarted) { if (r instanceof Future<?> f) f.cancel(false); // a caller blocked in get() wakes up } return neverStarted; // log them, or replay them }

alt.html: fun stop(pool: ExecutorService, grace: Duration): List<Runnable> { pool.shutdown() // no new work; the queue keeps draining try { if (pool.awaitTermination(grace.toNanos(), TimeUnit.NANOSECONDS)) return emptyList() } catch (e: InterruptedException) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt() // keep the flag, then stop hard } val neverStarted = pool.shutdownNow() // interrupts the running tasks neverStarted.forEach { (it as? Future<*>)?.cancel(false) } // a caller blocked in get() wakes up return neverStarted // log them, or replay them }

recap: Size a pool with Little's law: threads = peak rate x time per task, queue = peak rate x the longest wait you accept. Then check what sits behind the pool, whose own limit may be lower.
Bound the queue, set core equal to max, name the threads, and choose the rejection policy on purpose: for money, count and throw, never drop.
Shut down in order: shutdown, awaitTermination with a deadline, then shutdownNow. Cancel what it returns, and log or replay those transfers. None may vanish.
Journal first, apply second, and never wait inside apply. Then an interrupt can only stop a transfer that hasn't changed anything yet.
A sum of separately locked reads is torn. A whole snapshot holds every lock in the global order, copies, and publishes a record that never changes through one volatile write.
Where this pool stops: it suits short journal writes, not requests that mostly wait. And a pool stuck waiting on itself shows only as named threads parked on a FutureTask, with no deadlock report.

explain.prompt: A colleague asks why the ledger pool has only 8 threads and 80 queue slots when the machine has memory for thousands. Explain where both numbers come from, and what happens when traffic goes above the plan.
explain.answer: Both come from Little's law. At the planned peak of 1,600 transfers a second, each transfer holds a thread for about 5 ms while the journal writes it, so 1,600 x 0.005 = 8 transfers are in flight. Eight threads keep up, and more would only wait on the same journal. The queue absorbs bursts, but every queued transfer waits: a busy pool finishes 1,600 a second, so 80 queued transfers wait at most 50 ms, the longest wait we accept. A bigger queue would hide seconds of waiting until customers give up and try again. Above the plan, the queue fills, and the counting policy turns the extra transfers away at once: the customer gets a fast "busy, try again", sends the same transfer id again, and the count shows the overload on the dashboard. If that happens often, we measure the journal again and resize, or make each journal write carry more transfers.

deeper.html:
Locking every account costs time in proportion to the number of accounts, and it stops every transfer while it copies. At 50 accounts that is microseconds. At five million accounts, it is a pause customers feel. Three designs avoid it.

A snapshot per group. Split the accounts into groups, send every transfer to one group, and snapshot each group on its own. The grand total is the sum of the group totals, which stays exact only while no transfer crosses from one group to another.

Copy-on-write state. Keep all balances in one map that never changes, behind an AtomicReference, and make every transfer a compare-and-set of a new map. Readers get a whole snapshot for free with get(). Writers pay for the copy and try again when another writer won, so this fits books that are read often and written rarely. It is the printed price board from Don't share: immutability, confinement, ThreadLocal, used for writes too:

Java
private final AtomicReference<Map<String, Long>> balances =
        new AtomicReference<>(Map.of("alice", 100L, "bob", 0L));

boolean transfer(String from, String to, long cents) {
    while (true) {
        Map<String, Long> now = balances.get();                   // a whole snapshot, for free
        if (now.get(from) < cents) return false;
        Map<String, Long> next = new HashMap<>(now);              // copy, change two entries
        next.merge(from, -cents, Long::sum);
        next.merge(to, cents, Long::sum);
        if (balances.compareAndSet(now, Map.copyOf(next))) return true;   // try again if another writer won
    }
}
Kotlin
private val balances = AtomicReference(mapOf("alice" to 100L, "bob" to 0L))

fun transfer(from: String, to: String, cents: Long): Boolean {
    while (true) {
        val now = balances.get()                                  // a whole snapshot, for free
        if (now.getValue(from) < cents) return false
        val next = now + mapOf(from to now.getValue(from) - cents, to to now.getValue(to) + cents)
        if (balances.compareAndSet(now, next)) return true        // try again if another writer won
    }
}

Building from the journal. Treat the journal as the truth, and a snapshot as the result of applying it up to some position. That style is called event sourcing. You can build snapshots on another machine that reads the journal, and the live ledger never stops for them.

For dumps, jcmd <pid> Thread.dump_to_file -format=json <file> writes the same information as JSON, a text format that tools can group and count. Lesson 3 of this track uses it on 10,000 virtual threads.
